content: The glottis refers to the space between the vocal cords. When the vocal cords vibrate, this vibration generates a buzzing quality in speech, which is referred to as voice or voicing. Sound production that involves only the glottis is termed glottal. In the English language, there exists a voiceless glottal fricative, represented by the letter h. In many English accents, the glottal stop, which is produced by pressing the vocal folds together, is used as a variant allophone of the phoneme /t/ (and in some dialects, occasionally of /k/ and /p/). In certain languages, the glottal stop functions as an independent phoneme. Skilled players of the Australian didgeridoo manipulate their glottal opening to control and produce the full range of timbres available on the instrument. The vibration of the vocal cords is a critical component in the production of voiced consonants as well as vowels. When the vocal folds are drawn apart, air flows between them without causing vibration, as is the case in the production of voiceless consonants. Voiced consonants include sounds such as /b/, /d/, and /g/. Voiceless consonants include sounds such as /p/, /t/, and /k/. The larynx, which houses the vocal cords, can be visualized from behind, showing the entrance to the larynx.
